choices.A: Research reveals that web architecture among species of Tetragnatha spiders has likely diversified more rapidly than the material properties of Tetragnatha’s silk have.
choices.B: Research suggests that the material properties of silk from species of Tetragnatha spiders have diversified during adaptive radiation.
choices.C: A study indicates that variations in web architecture among species of Tetragnatha spiders can likely be explained by corresponding variations in the material properties of their silks.
choices.D: A study shows that adaptive radiation can explain interspecies variation in the web architecture of Tetragnatha spiders but not in the material properties of the spiders’ silk.

rationale: Choice B is the best answer because it most accurately states the main idea of the text. The text notes that Tetragnatha spiders have diversified their web architecture, or web design, through adaptive radiation and that Alicea-Serrano et al. investigated whether silk material properties were also affected by this process. After examining chemical composition, tensile strength, and viscosity of silks from three Tetragnatha species, the team found significant interspecies variation in these material properties, meaning that there were observable differences in these traits across the studied species. In the context of the study’s research question, this finding suggests that the material properties of silk from species of Tetragnatha spiders have indeed diversified during adaptive radiation, which is the main idea of the text.

Choice A is incorrect because the text doesn’t compare the rate of diversification in web architecture to the rate of diversification in silk properties. Although the text notes that web architecture diversified “over a relatively short timescale,” it doesn’t make a corresponding temporal claim about silk properties or suggest that one changed more rapidly than the other. Choice C is incorrect because the study investigated silk properties as a separate question, not as an explanation for differences in web architecture. The researchers discussed in the text investigated whether silk properties were “similarly affected” by adaptive radiation, not whether they caused the variations in web design. Choice D is incorrect because it contradicts the findings described in the text. The study found “significant interspecies variation” in silk biomaterials, suggesting that adaptive radiation did affect the properties of Tetragnatha spiders’ silk rather than showing that adaptive radiation cannot explain silk variation.
stem: Through adaptive radiation, multiple species of Tetragnatha—a genus of orb-weaving spiders—have significantly diversified their web architecture over a relatively short timescale. To investigate whether the material properties of Tetragnatha silk have been similarly affected by this evolutionary process, Angela M. Alicea-Serrano et al. examined the chemical composition of both the radial (non-sticky threads extending from the center) and capture (sticky threads that hold prey) silks that form the web as well as tested the tensile strength and viscosity of samples collected from three Tetragnatha species at two sites in the Hawaiian archipelago. The team found significant interspecies variation in these biomaterials.
